summary: Recommends using 127-bit IPv6 prefixes on point-to-point links between routers, similar to 31-bit prefixes in IPv4, and explains the motivation. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Two routers on a private cable only need two addresses. Using a tiny address block leaves nothing extra for troublemakers.

subtitle: Why router-to-router IPv6 links should use a /127 prefix, and the rules that make it safe.

tldr.problem: Earlier advice discouraged 127-bit IPv6 prefixes on router links, yet 64-bit prefixes on those links open the door to forwarding loops and neighbor cache exhaustion attacks.
tldr.mechanism: Routers MUST support assigning /127 prefixes on point-to-point inter-router links and MUST disable Subnet-Router anycast for the prefix. Operators who number links out of a /64 should avoid a few reserved addresses.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track document that reverses the earlier discouragement and parallels the use of 31-bit prefixes in IPv4. It is updated by RFC 6547.

facts.label: Router requirement
facts.value: MUST support /127 and disable Subnet-Router anycast

today: RFC 6164 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6547. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the base recommendation for /127 prefixes on inter-router links, with RFC 6547 applied on top.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4291 says interface IDs for most IPv6 unicast addresses must be 64 bits long, and it defines the Subnet-Router anycast address, meant for reaching any one of the routers on a link.

Some operators have used 127-bit prefixes anyway, although this was discouraged because of conflicts with Subnet-Router anycast. RFC 6164 gives the rationale for /127 on inter-router links, reevaluates why it was thought harmful, and specifies how to use it. It parallels the use of 31-bit prefixes in IPv4.
sections.eli5: The rule book said every street must have room for a huge number of houses. But a street with only two houses does not need that much room, and the extra room causes trouble.

sections.title: Scope of the Recommendation
sections.content:
The document applies where operators assign specific addresses on inter-router point-to-point links instead of relying on link-local addresses. Operators do this for network monitoring, reverse DNS for traceroute and other tools, EBGP peering sessions and so on.

An inter-router point-to-point link is a link with only two routers and no hosts attached. It can include Ethernet links configured to be point-to-point. Router-to-host links and links with both routers and hosts are out of scope, and so is the link-local address scope.
sections.eli5: This only covers a cable that joins exactly two routers. It is not about cables that also have computers plugged in.

sections.title: Why /127 Was Discouraged
sections.content:
RFC 3627 discouraged 127-bit prefixes because of conflicts with Subnet-Router anycast addresses, while noting that the usefulness of Subnet-Router anycast on point-to-point links is questionable. RFC 5375 also called /127 not valid and to be strongly discouraged, but its stated reason was compliance with RFC 3627.

RFC 6164 accepts that those analyses were correct, but says operational experience with IPv6 has shown that /127 prefixes can be used successfully.
sections.eli5: People once said "do not do that" for a good reason. Later, many tried it and found it works fine.

sections.title: Problems with Longer-than-Needed Prefixes
sections.content:
Ping-pong. On a point-to-point link with a prefix shorter than 127, a forwarding loop can occur. Interfaces that use Neighbor Discovery are not affected, but links such as SONET do not use it, so any prefix shorter than 127 bits there can create an attack vector. RFC 4443 mitigates this: a router MUST NOT forward such a packet back on the link it arrived on, and SHOULD send an ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable (code 3). That check is on the forwarding path and may affect performance.

Neighbor cache exhaustion. On an Ethernet link with a /64, a packet to any unassigned address makes the forwarding router create a cache entry in INCOMPLETE state and send a Neighbor Solicitation. An attacker sending to many of the 2^64 - 3 unassigned addresses can use up memory and processing. Rate-limiting reduces but is unlikely to neutralize the attack, and if the link goes down during an attack, sessions such as BGP might never be re-established. Assigning /127 subnets eliminates the problem completely.

Other reasons. Some operators prefer not to give a /64 to each link and number all point-to-point links out of one /64 or a few.
sections.eli5: If a street has billions of empty house numbers, a prankster can send you to knock on all of them and keep you busy. If the street has only two houses, there is nobody to prank you with.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
Routers MUST support assigning /127 prefixes on point-to-point inter-router links. Routers MUST disable Subnet-Router anycast for the prefix when /127 is used.

When many links are numbered out of one /64, care is needed so reserved anycast addresses are not assigned as unicast addresses. Two rules apply:

  • Addresses with all zeros in the rightmost 64 bits SHOULD NOT be assigned as unicast, to avoid colliding with the Subnet-Router anycast address.
  • Addresses where the rightmost 64 bits fall in the highest 128 values (ffff:ffff:ffff:ff7f to ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff) SHOULD NOT be used as unicast, to avoid colliding with the reserved subnet anycast addresses of RFC 2526.
sections.eli5: Routers must be willing to use the tiny two-house street. And a few special house numbers are kept for the post office, so nobody should live there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it has no inherent security considerations of its own. It does discuss security-related issues, namely the neighbor cache exhaustion and ping-pong problems above, and proposes /127 as the solution to them.
sections.eli5: The RFC is itself a safety measure, so its only security story is the trouble it helps you avoid.
